of the final action to be a string. The correction admits a different type of the
\texttt{answer} field: a failed task is credited if and only if (i) its failure tags are
non-empty and contained in \{\texttt{final\_answer\_missing}, \texttt{schema\_violation},
\texttt{invalid\_json}, \texttt{final\_answer\_shape\_violation}\}, (ii) an \texttt{answer}
value can be recovered from the parsed action or from the raw model output, and (iii) that
value is not a \texttt{str} and one of the golden strings of the task occurs as a substring of
its Python \texttt{str()} rendering. Any non-string type qualifies; the types actually observed
are \texttt{float} for Bielik-11B and \texttt{dict} or \texttt{float} for Bielik-7B. The paper
reports both rates side by side as a sensitivity analysis and does not pick one of them as the
benchmark result: the corrected rate comes from \texttt{analysis/ladder\_typing\_tolerant.py},

{\footnotesize
\begin{minipage}{0.97\linewidth}
$\Delta$ rate is the corrected rate minus the strict rate. It is non-zero on rung L3N only:
on L0, L1, L2 and L3T the strict and the corrected counts are identical in all eight runs, and
all 20 credited tasks are L3N. The correction is not a blanket amnesty for format failures:
across the same eight runs 110 failures carry exactly the same format-only tag profile, of
which 20 are credited and the remaining 90 are not. Those 90 fail on three distinct grounds,
not one: in 59 an \texttt{answer} value is recovered and is not a \texttt{str}, but no golden
string of the task occurs in its \texttt{str()} rendering, so criterion (iii) is not met; in
29 no \texttt{answer} value can be recovered from the parsed action or the raw output at all,
so criterion (ii) is not met; and in the remaining 2 the recovered value is itself a
\texttt{str}, which criterion (iii) excludes, since a string \texttt{answer} is exactly what
the strict schema already accepts.
\end{minipage}}
